extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers; writers and critics of essays, satire, theatre-goers and moralists (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing satirical and humorous essays and moral criticism (choice of targets, nature of humour, theatrical representation, and the proper cultivation of beauty and reading).

rubrics_metrics.name: True art of assisting beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The true Art of assisting Beauty consists in Embellishing the whole Person by the proper Ornaments of virtuous and commendable Qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is enhanced primarily by moral and mental qualities (innocence, piety, good humour, truth). Physical colouring and art ('Colours, artfully spread upon Canvas') may entertain the eye, but do not affect the heart; virtues 'beautify her Beauty.' Example quotes: 'Grace was in all her Steps, Heaven in her Eye.' Anti-pattern: treating beauty as purely visual ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce women to mere objects of sight
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a low and degrading Idea of that Sex ... to consider them meerly as Objects of Sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid portraying women only by external appearance or as paintings; esteem and love arise when beauty is 'heighten'd by Virtue.' Practical implication for writers: present female characters with inward qualities as the source of their charm rather than only outward features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire target principle — attack vice, not particular persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Scourge Vice and Folly as they appear in a Multitude, without condescending to be a Publisher of particular Intrigues and Cuckoldoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim satire at general vices and collective follies rather than exposing private intrigues or naming individuals. 'Assault the Vice without hurting the Person.' Promise: 'never to draw a faulty Character which does not fit at least a Thousand People.' Anti-pattern: publishing particulars that shame private individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid aggravating the poor and already depressed (don't punch down)
rubrics_metrics.description: My Paper would only serve to aggravate the Pains of Poverty, if it chiefly expos'd those who are already depressed, and in some measure turn'd into Ridicule, by the Meanness of their Conditions and Circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from directing ridicule chiefly at the indigent or socially helpless; satire that targets the already disadvantaged only compounds their suffering and is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack vices in high and conspicuous stations when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Vice and Folly ought to be attacked where-ever they could be met with, and especially when they were placed in high and conspicuous Stations of Life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominent persons who display vice are legitimate objects of public reprehension because their example is influential. Balance this with the principle of avoiding needless personal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose targets with regard to readers and social role
rubrics_metrics.description: Different speakers in the Club advise caution about meddling with particular groups (e.g., Country Squires, the Army, Inns of Court), noting local sensibilities: 'let me tell you, some of them take it ill of you that you mention Fox-hunters with so little Respect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the audience, local customs, and potential backlash when selecting satirical targets; certain groups may reasonably expect different treatment. This is pragmatic guidance about scope rather than a moral exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour must be under the check of reason and regularity of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour should always lye under the Check of Reason, and ... it requires the Direction of the nicest Judgment, by so much the more as it indulges it self in the most boundless Freedoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good humour balances freedom and constraint: it permits wildness but within coherent, reasoned structure. Anti-patterns: delirious mirth, incoherent fantastical conceits, or nonsense presented as humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of True Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: True Humour is the offspring of GOOD SENSE (from TRUTH) and the issue of WIT married to MIRTH; it 'never fails to make his Company laugh' and 'generally looks serious, whilst every Body laughs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True humour mixes seriousness and mirth, is rooted in truth and good sense, aims to instruct or illuminate as well as entertain, and often appears grave while provoking laughter. Evaluate humour by its balance of wit and mirth and its descent from truthful, sensible premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of False Humour (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: False Humour descends from FALSEHOOD → NONSENSE → FRENZY and differs from the true as a Monkey does from a Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize false humour by these traits (listed in the essay): (1) given to apish tricks and buffooneries; (2) delights in mimicry indiscriminately exposing virtue or vice; (3) unlucky — ridicules friends and foes alike out of small talent; (4) void of reason, pursues no moral or instructive point and is ludicrous for its own sake; (5) ridicule is personal and aimed at the man or writer rather than the vice or writing. Anti-patterns include loud excessive laughter that does not bring others with it and works that are incoherent or merely frantic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake extravagant conceits or incoherence for humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ... raving incoherent Pieces ... are rather the Offsprings of a Distempered Brain, than Works of Humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid valuing novelty, wildness, or monstrous conceits alone; coherence and reason are necessary. If writing provokes pity for the author rather than laughter, it is failed humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise of proportion in satirical character-drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: I promise him, never to draw a faulty Character which does not fit at least a Thousand People; or to publish a single Paper, that is not written in the Spirit of Benevolence and with a Love to Mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating satirical types, ensure that they represent broad, recognizable social archetypes rather than thinly veiled portraits of specific individuals; maintain benevolence as an ethical constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical representation should avoid grotesque monsters and show affectation as social product
rubrics_metrics.description: We ... intend for the future to show no Monsters, but Men who are converted into such by their own Industry and Affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On stage, prefer depicting human affectation and social artifice rather than spectacles of 'monsters.' Theatrical satire should expose affectation and learned absurdities among the polite and well-bred rather than relying on gross monstrosities for entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of reading for improvement (advice for ladies)
rubrics_metrics.description: What Improvements would a Woman have made, who is so Susceptible of Impressions from what she reads, had she been guided to such Books as have a Tendency to enlighten the Understanding and rectify the Passions, as well as to those which are of little more use than to divert the Imagination?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend books that enlighten understanding and correct the passions (moral, religious, philosophical works) over romances and purely diverting reading. Practical implication: curate reading lists that foster virtue and reason.
